title: Errors vs Exceptions
summary: Master the critical distinction between java.lang.Error (fatal JVM failures) and java.lang.Exception (recoverable application conditions) under java.lang.Throwable.
learningOutcomes: Differentiate between catastrophic system errors and recoverable application exceptions
Avoid dangerous catch-all anti-patterns in production

activities.title: Core Mechanics: Errors vs Exceptions

breakdown.details: The ultimate superclass of all errors and exceptions in the Java language.
Fatal system/JVM conditions indicating catastrophic failures. Applications should not attempt recovery.
Conditions that a reasonable application should catch, handle, or recover from.
Catching Throwable or Error masks fatal JVM problems, leading to corrupted state.

activities.title: Concept Check & MCQ: Errors vs Exceptions

questions.question: What is the common superclass of both `Error` and `Exception` in Java?
options: java.lang.Object
java.lang.Throwable
java.lang.RuntimeException
java.lang.SystemError
questions.explanation: `java.lang.Throwable` is the root superclass of all errors and exceptions in the Java language hierarchy.

questions.question: What is the fundamental difference between an `Error` and an `Exception`?
options: Errors occur at compile-time; Exceptions occur at runtime
Errors represent fatal JVM conditions that applications should not catch; Exceptions represent conditions an application can reasonably handle
Errors are written in C; Exceptions are written in Java
There is no difference; they are synonyms
questions.explanation: Errors signify catastrophic JVM failures (OutOfMemoryError, StackOverflowError) from which recovery is generally impossible. Exceptions are recoverable application conditions.

questions.question: Which of the following is a subclass of `java.lang.Error`?
options: NullPointerException
ArithmeticException
StackOverflowError
IllegalArgumentException
questions.explanation: `StackOverflowError` is a subclass of `VirtualMachineError`, which extends `java.lang.Error`.

questions.question: Why is writing `catch (Error e)` or `catch (Throwable t)` considered a dangerous anti-pattern in application code?
options: It causes the compiler to crash
It can trap fatal JVM failures like OutOfMemoryError, preventing the JVM from terminating and leaving the app in a corrupted state
It makes the code run 10x slower
It is illegal syntax in Java 17
questions.explanation: Catching Error or Throwable masks fatal JVM conditions, continuing execution when memory or stack state is fatally corrupted.

questions.question: What causes an `OutOfMemoryError` in Java?
options: Opening too many browser tabs
The JVM Heap has exhausted available memory and the Garbage Collector cannot reclaim enough space to allocate an object
Dividing by zero in a loop
Using too many comments in code
questions.explanation: OutOfMemoryError occurs when the JVM cannot allocate an object because Heap memory is exhausted and Garbage Collection cannot free space.

questions.question: What causes a `StackOverflowError` in Java?
options: Allocating an array of 1 million elements on the Heap
Excessive deep or infinite method recursion that exhausts the thread Call Stack memory
Writing to a read-only hard drive
Importing too many packages
questions.explanation: StackOverflowError happens when method calls recurse infinitely or too deeply, pushing stack frames until the thread's Stack memory limit is exceeded.

questions.question: Which of the following belongs to the `Exception` branch rather than the `Error` branch?
options: OutOfMemoryError
NoClassDefFoundError
InternalError
FileNotFoundException
questions.explanation: `FileNotFoundException` is a subclass of `IOException`, which extends `java.lang.Exception`.

questions.question: Can you instantiate an `Error` object manually in Java code (`new Error("test")`)?
options: No, Error constructors are private
Yes, but it is rarely appropriate in standard application software
Only within JVM native C code
Only when running as root/administrator
questions.explanation: Error has public constructors and can be instantiated, but doing so in standard business applications is almost always incorrect.

interviewQA.question: What is the key difference between Error and Exception in Java?
interviewQA.answer: Both inherit from `Throwable`. `Error` represents serious, unrecoverable system conditions caused by the JVM or underlying environment (e.g. `OutOfMemoryError`, `StackOverflowError`). Applications should not attempt to catch `Error`. `Exception` represents conditions caused by application logic (e.g. `IOException`, `NullPointerException`) from which an application can reasonably recover.

interviewQA.question: Can you catch an Error with a try-catch block? Is it recommended?
interviewQA.answer: Syntactically, yes: `catch (Error e)` or `catch (Throwable t)` will compile and execute. However, it is strongly discouraged in application code. When an Error occurs (such as memory exhaustion), the internal integrity of the JVM is compromised. Catching it and continuing execution usually leads to silent data corruption or cascading deadlocks.

interviewQA.question: What is the difference between OutOfMemoryError and StackOverflowError?
interviewQA.answer: `OutOfMemoryError` occurs when the JVM **Heap** is full and the Garbage Collector cannot free enough memory to satisfy an allocation request. `StackOverflowError` occurs when a thread's **Call Stack** memory is exhausted, almost always due to infinite or excessively deep recursive method calls.

interviewQA.question: What is NoClassDefFoundError and how does it differ from ClassNotFoundException?
interviewQA.answer: `ClassNotFoundException` is an `Exception` thrown when an application attempts to load a class dynamically at runtime (e.g. `Class.forName("...")`) and the `.class` file cannot be found. `NoClassDefFoundError` is an `Error` thrown when a class was available at compile-time, but during runtime execution, the class definition is missing from the classpath.

interviewQA.question: What are some scenarios where catching Throwable is acceptable?
interviewQA.answer: Catching `Throwable` is acceptable only in top-level framework infrastructure: 1) Thread pool executors (to prevent worker threads from silently terminating), 2) Web server entry points (to log an uncaught disaster and return a 500 HTTP response), and 3) Global logging crash-reporters.

interviewQA.question: Why does ThreadDeath extend Error rather than Exception?
interviewQA.answer: `ThreadDeath` is thrown when a thread is stopped via the legacy `Thread.stop()` method. It extends `Error` so that normal user `catch (Exception e)` blocks will not inadvertently intercept it, allowing the thread to terminate cleanly.

interviewQA.question: What is VirtualMachineError?
interviewQA.answer: `VirtualMachineError` is an abstract subclass of `Error`. It is thrown by the JVM to indicate that the virtual machine is broken or has run out of resources necessary for it to continue operating. Its prominent subclasses are `OutOfMemoryError`, `StackOverflowError`, `InternalError`, and `UnknownError`.

I know why applications should never catch Error in business logic.
I understand the causes of OutOfMemoryError and StackOverflowError.
I know that Throwable is the root superclass of both branches.
I can identify which conditions are recoverable vs catastrophic.
